conclusion.honest_verdict: The room thinks the bones of Numbite's onboarding are right but too much has been piled on them, and it averaged 5.8 out of 10. The best screens are the cover's moving wall of real logos and the first-recipe cards, which show real dishes with a price per serving and the protein for your meal; one question per screen, stone and pounds, and targets that arrive filled in and can be changed also work. But people must make an account before they see a single number. They then read about 230 words of tour that Pip's Home tips repeat almost word for word, watch the counter start again three times, are told 'You're all set!' at step 8 of 9, and reach their first restaurant number at about touch 55. Several faults make it look unfinished: on 'Your size' the grey-button hint is printed over the privacy promise, confetti falls over the plan card, the plate picture is cut off twice, and Pip says 'Great choice.' only for Lose weight. A bug also saves the untouched starting numbers as the person's own targets when they skip the body questions. Money is muddled too: in the 1.1 build the + button adds a meal for free, yet Home says 'Log your meals to see what's left today. See Pro', the new week and labels pages say the same, and Today is paywalled. That mismatch, more than the paywall itself, is why testers felt tricked, and nobody has yet tried the real path, because every test round used the build with sign-in switched off.
conclusion.pip_verdict:
The room liked Pip but nobody remembered him (6.2). He is friendly, has no link to any food or brand and never preaches. His walk along the tab bar and his squash-and-stretch landing are the best moments in the flow, and nobody wants a body shape that could ever look thinner or fatter. Close up, the drawing has faults:
- His cheeks look grey-brown.
- His 'think' arm is drawn inside his body, so he looks one-armed and seems to roll his eyes.
- 'Point' aims at nothing.
- His arms are thin dark sticks.
- His moods look the same at 52 to 64 px.
- He bobs, waves and cheers forever.
His words are the bigger problem. He repeats the heading, ends nearly every line with '!' and promises 'a few quick questions' before nine steps. He also praises only one goal ('Great choice.' for Lose weight), which goes against the spirit of your 13 November 'no GREAT CHOICE' rule. Fix the drawing, let him settle after a few seconds and give him calm, useful words that treat every answer the same, and he becomes the guide you wanted.
best_things: The cover's moving wall of real restaurant and shop logos, with '241 UK restaurants' and '9 supermarkets': it says what the app is in two seconds, before a word is read.

The first-recipe cards: two real dishes fitted to the meal of the day, with calories, protein, minutes and '£x a serving' from real supermarket products. Ten of 16 called it the most persuasive screen.
Pip walking along a copy of the real tab bar. The bubble's tail follows him, and the bubble keeps one height so nothing jumps. Ten named it their favourite moment.
One question per screen and big tiles. Stone and pounds and feet and inches come by default, and one tap switches to kg and cm, converting exactly.
Targets that arrive filled in and can all be edited, with calm cautions, a 1,200 kcal floor, the under-18 path (no weight asked) and Pip's 'only a starting point'.
A privacy promise that is true: sex, age, height, weight and activity live only in the page's memory and are never stored or sent.
Sign in with Apple comes first, and the email code says 'There's no password to remember', with the iPhone's one-time-code autofill.
Pip's tips on the real screens: one real button lit at a time, VoiceOver-friendly, 'Stop the tips' that really stops them, and a replay in Settings.
Reduced motion stops every animation through one global rule, and the 0.6 s guard stops a double tap from skipping a screen unseen.
The shops screen: every supermarket's logo with its name beside it. People found it a two-second screen.
worst_things: The account comes on screen 2, before any number. The sign-in screen says 'new or returning' three times, while the reason to sign in and the privacy promise sit at the bottom in 13 px grey. 'What your account syncs' is jargon.

The tour's 'What you can do' lists: 16 rows and about 230 words about buttons people haven't seen yet. The last row sits under Continue on every stop, and Pip's Home tips then say nearly the same sentences again.

The finish line keeps moving: a 7-segment bar, then 'Step 1 of 9', then 'Tip 1 of 7'. 'A few quick questions' turns out to be nine steps, and 'You're all set!' comes at step 8 of 9, followed by 'Choose a recipe' above a 'Take me to Home' button.

Visible faults: on 'Your size' the grey-button hint is printed over the privacy promise, confetti falls over the plan card, and the plate picture is cut off on the targets screen and on 'You're all set!'.

Money is muddled. In the 1.1 build, + is free, but:
- Home shows 'Log your meals to see what's left today. See Pro'.
- The new week and labels pages say the numbers 'show here once you log your meals'.
- Today is fully paywalled.
- 'See Pro' sits next to 'Premium' badges.
- The trial sheet opens 1.2 s after the last tip.

Pip praises only one goal ('Great choice.' for Lose weight) and cheers over a calorie cut. He repeats every heading and ends lines with '!'. About allergens he says only 'Noted! I'll leave those out of your top picks.', with no caveat.
Answers are picked for people (Maintain, Lightly active). The four activity levels have no examples, though they change calories by up to 44%.

A bug undoes a round-2 fix. Skipping the body questions and pressing Continue on the untouched starting numbers saves hasSetTargets: true, which hides 'These are starting numbers' and Home's set-your-targets card.
Pip's drawing: grey-brown cheeks, a one-armed, eye-rolling 'think' face (used on About you and How active), a 'point' that aims at nothing, and moods that can't be told apart at small sizes.
Motion that never stops: Pip's bob, wave and cheer, the cover's count pills and the logo wall loop for as long as the screen is open, beside text people are reading.

Nobody has seen the real path. Every test round and these pictures used the build with sign-in switched off, so 'No account needed' and the 'It's optional' card were judged instead of the real screens.

Bringing back the text size screen: Standard only (founder 2026-11-19).

A complete list of every paid feature on the last screen, or new Premium badges on every paid button: the line says 'such as', and the paid buttons already say 'Unlock the other {n}' or 'Get Premium', or carry the Premium badge.

founder_questions: 1. Everyone still signs in. Can the sign-in screen move from screen 2 to straight after 'Your daily targets', as 'Save your plan: make your free account', still before Home so nobody reaches the app unsigned? 14 of 16 raised it, and the ex-reviewer thinks it also lowers the App Review 5.1.1(v) risk. The welcome screens already open without an account (signInGate). What it needs is a sync rule: a brand-new account keeps the goal, targets, diet and shops just typed on the phone, and an existing account's own numbers are never overwritten by them. The cover's new 'Already have an account? Sign in' link lets returning people sign in before answering again. Recommended: yes, and if you agree, in this same pass.

2. Is adding meals free or paid in 1.1?
- **Free, according to:** the code (PAID_TIER_ONLY), your 13 November brief, docs/PAYMENTS.md and the 1.1 'What's New' ('Everything that was free stays free').
- **Paid, according to:** your 11 October answer, 'logging stays Pro'.
- **Build 7 today:** in review, it still shows 'Log your meals... See Pro' on Home and paywalls Today, while + adds a meal for free.

Recommended: free. Home, Today and the week and labels pages now follow the gate, so either answer is one line, but that change goes into no binary until you answer. Fix it in the next build unless App Review raises it.

3. Pro or Premium as the one name (already open)? Home's 'See Pro' and 'Try Pro free' sit next to 'Premium' badges, the trial sheet and the tips, and ten testers noticed both on one screen. Recommended: Premium everywhere ('See Premium', 'Try Premium free').

4. You chose 'Sign in or sign up' on 18 November. Seven stumbled on the look-alike pair: Margaret, the dyslexic tester, Marta, the dietitian, the copywriter, the student and the growth expert. Recommended: keep one screen, but let its heading follow the button pressed: 'Make your free account' from Get started, 'Welcome back. Sign in' from the cover's 'Already have an account? Sign in'. If you'd rather keep 'Sign in or sign up', it stays as built.

5. The one-time trial sheet opens about 1.2 s after the last Home tip (your 16 November decision), at the end of about 40 touches. The ex-reviewer and the growth expert said the first free moment becomes an offer to pay. Recommended: show it the first time someone taps a Premium feature, or on their second visit, never straight after setup.

6. Pip's look: in October's flat redesign he kept his glossy shading, and four testers now say it clashes. Several read him as an apple, lime or pea. Recommended: add a flat two-tone Pip (one green, one shade crescent, a small highlight, the new outline) to the comparison sheet made for the redraw, next to today's Pip and the new one, before anything more changes. Keep the round body: the dietitian asked that he never have a shape that could look thinner or fatter.

7. Keep 'Hi, I'm Pip!' as its own screen (your 15 October 'cool animation' moment), or have Pip jump straight onto the Home stop to save a tap? Ten asked to merge; the designers, the dyslexic tester and the accessibility tester asked to keep it. Recommended: keep it, now with a useful line that arrives sooner.

8. App Review fallback: NEXT_PUBLIC_SIGN_IN_REQUIRED=0 is baked into the packed app, so a 5.1.1(v) rejection of build 7 means a new archive and a second review. Recommended: a small remote switch on numbite.com, read like the logo take-down list, that can only ever make sign-in optional, never stricter. It needs your go-ahead, because it touches rule 4's fallback.

9. The GLP-1 goal (health), halal (religion) and allergies sync to the account, stored in the US. Under UK GDPR these are likely special-category data. Recommended: add them to the solicitor's questions in docs/LEGAL_REVIEW_PACK.md. Until then nothing changes, and the new targets and sign-in lines say plainly what is saved with the account.

10. May we count how many people reach each setup screen, anonymously, with the pre-approved TelemetryDeck (screen reached only, no personal data)? The next round would then be based on real drop-off rather than 16 simulated people. Turning it on means rewording four things together: the cover's 'No ads, no tracking', the sign-in screen's 'No ads, no tracking', the privacy page's 'Neither sends usage statistics' and STORE.md's 'no analytics in this version'. The goal is that an ordinary reader would not call the counts tracking, without leaning on Apple's narrow definition. Recommended: yes, with those rewordings, the privacy page and the App Privacy answers updated first.

11. Snacks show '0 kcal' on Home because the day is split 25/35/40 across breakfast, lunch and dinner. The dietitian says that reads as 'snacks aren't allowed'. Recommended: add the line 'Snacks come out of what's left' under Snacks now (no constant change). Give snacks a share only if you want to change the split (rule 8).

12. The dietitian and the GLP-1 user questioned some target constants: a 500 kcal cut for someone with a low BMI who picks Lose weight, the same 1,200 floor for men and women, and the full −500 on the GLP-1 plan. Recommended: keep them for 1.1, and have a registered dietitian review them before any change (rule 8).

13. The cover's logo wall moves for about 50 s a pass and never stops, and WCAG 2.2.2 asks that motion beside text can be paused. Everything else on the welcome screens now settles within 5 s. Recommended: a small 44 pt 'Pause' button at the wall's corner. The wall keeps moving until someone taps it, as you wanted, and reduced motion already stops it.
